screens.title: GRAMMAR: Comparisons
screens.subtitle: 1. Read this short text about the fashion industry and answer the questions.
screens.text: Why is it that fashion houses design their clothes for the youngest and skinniest men and women? We may not actually want to look like supermodels, but it is a fact that the most underweight models have dominated the world’s catwalks for a very long time. It seems it is not in the interests of the fashion industry to represent an ‘average’ person. Although ‘slimmer’ may not always mean ‘more desirable’ in the real world, fashion succeeds because it carries with it that image of the least achievable figure.
items: 1. What is the text about?
2. How does the writer feel about the fashion industry?
3. What comparison structures are used in the text?
presentationExpected: The fashion industry and its preference for the youngest/thinnest models.
screens.answer: 1. The fashion industry and its preference for the youngest/thinnest models. · 2. The writer seems critical/disapproving. · 3. Comparative and superlative structures.

screens.title: GRAMMAR: Comparisons
screens.subtitle: 2. These comparison structures are used with adjectives.
items: a. Why do we say *younger than* but *less serious than*; and *the youngest* but *the most underweight*?
b. Which common adjectives can we either add *-er / -est* to or use *more / most* with?
c. What are the spelling rules for *slim* and *skinny*?
presentationExpected: Short adjectives usually take -er/-est; longer adjectives use more/most/less/least.
Some two-syllable adjectives can use either form, e.g. clever, simple, narrow.
screens.answer: a. Short adjectives usually take -er/-est; longer adjectives use more/most/less/least. · b. Some two-syllable adjectives can use either form, e.g. clever, simple, narrow. · c. slim → slimmer/slimmest; skinny → skinnier/skinniest.

screens.title: GRAMMAR: Comparisons
screens.subtitle: 6. Identify the comparative adverbs in this short newspaper article and explain how they are formed.
presentationExpected: Comparative adverbs: much lower, far more readily, less exclusively, less seriously. Formation: comparative forms are modified by degree adverbs such as much, far and less.
screens.text: Counterfeit consumer goods – more commonly known as ‘knock-offs’ – are imitation goods that are offered for sale at much lower prices than the genuine products, and they are a big problem for the fashion industry. Knock-offs are now far more readily available than they were a few years ago, both on the web and on market stalls worldwide. These fake designer goods damage the actual brands in more ways than one, reducing their sales and causing them to be regarded less exclusively, no longer the luxury items they once were. Some people view the matter less seriously, arguing that knock-offs offer a type of free advertising and promotion to the real designer labels. However, there is no getting away from the fact that this is an illegal activity, and the fashion industry is starting to fight back with high-tech solutions that will distinguish the real goods from cheap copies.
screens.answer: Comparative adverbs include much lower, far more readily, less exclusively and less seriously. Discuss how the adverbs modify comparative forms in context.

screens.subtitle: 8. Practise comparison structures by completing the second sentences so that they have a similar meaning to the first. Use the word given.
items: 1. Mary is shorter than her brother. (NOT) → Mary is | her brother.
2. These sunglasses cost a bit less than my last pair. (WERE) → These sunglasses | than my last pair.
3. Very few designers were as talented as Coco Chanel. (MOST) → Coco Chanel was one of | in the world.
4. I preferred you with curlier hair. (STRAIGHT) → I preferred your hair when it wasn’t |.
5. This shoe shop is the cheapest one I’ve found. (EXPENSIVE) → This shoe shop is | all the ones I’ve found.
6. Suzanne’s host wasn’t as elegantly dressed as she was. (MORE) → Suzanne was far | her host.
7. It takes much less time to travel by train than by car. (LOT) → Travelling by train | travelling by car.
8. Harry wears smarter clothes now he has a girlfriend. (LESS) → Harry dressed | he didn’t have a girlfriend.
9. That model is only 17 – I thought she was older. (AS) → That model is not | I thought.

screens.title: READING
screens.subtitle: 4. Look at the photo of a pair of jeans. How old do you think they are today? Read the text quickly to find out.
screens.text:
$25,000 may sound excessive for a tatty pair of jeans, but the ones in this picture are not an ordinary pair of Levi’s. They are said to be one of the two oldest pairs left. They are certainly the most expensive!

Discovered last year in an old coal mine in Colorado, they were initially sold for $10,000 and then sold on again at a higher price. Then Seth Weisser paid even more for them. Co-owner of a store appropriately called What Comes Around Goes Around, he decided to contact Levi’s in San Francisco. ‘I sent them pictures of the jeans and they were delighted. They would have paid $40,000, I think!’

Levi’s has its own museum and Lynn Downey, the company historian, said: ‘I knew this would be a treasure that the company would want us to have, so Levi’s agreed to pay one of the highest sums ever for a pair of old jeans.’

Apart from a hole in the left pocket and frayed edges at the bottom, the jeans are in remarkably good condition for their age. Ms Downey was able to date them by their leather patch, which was added in 1886, and the single back pocket. A second pocket was added in 1902. She said: ‘Perhaps the most important reason why Levi’s bought these jeans is that the company lost everything in the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and the first 50 years of our history was destroyed.’
evidence: their leather patch, which was added in 1886
A second pocket was added in 1902

mcq.q: How old are the jeans likely to be?

screens.answer: C. They were made sometime between 1886 and 1902. As of 2026, approximately 124–140 years old.

screens.title: CONSOLIDATION
screens.instruction: Check what you can now use confidently.

groups.heading: COMPARE
items: Form comparative and superlative adjectives accurately.
Use *more/less … than*, *the most/least …* and irregular forms.

groups.heading: MODIFY
items: Show small differences with *a bit / slightly*.
Show larger differences with *much / a lot / a great deal*; emphasise superlatives with *by far*.

groups.heading: USE IN CONTEXT
items: Use *as … as / not as … as*.
Recognise comparative adverbs, fashion vocabulary, spelling patterns and phrasal verbs.

screens.title: HOMEWORK
screens.instruction: Compare a formal outfit (a suit, shirt and tie) with a casual outfit (jeans, a T-shirt and trainers) in 80–100 words.
presentationExpected: Model answer: A formal outfit is much more elegant than a casual outfit, but it is not as comfortable as jeans, a T-shirt and trainers. A casual outfit is a lot easier to put together and is slightly more practical for everyday activities. However, a suit, shirt and tie may be more suitable for special occasions. I prefer the casual outfit because it is more comfortable and easier to wear.
items: Use at least four comparison structures from Unit 1.2.
Include one adverb of degree and one phrasal verb.
Finish with your personal preference and one reason.
